title: Kicker and fixed V
family: Compact rollers lift; fixed V guides orient
summary: Three transverse contacts pull coral over a supported ramp into fixed V guide banks and a low receiver. UNTESTED sketch proposal.
advantage: Separating pickup and orientation may keep the moving nose small and the receiver pose repeatable.
risk: A passive V can wedge a crosswise coral; contact gaps between the pickup, kicker and exit roll may cause dead spots.
firstTest: Hand-feed slow, offset and crosswise coral through a flat-stock mockup; check each contact transition and receiver-absent hold.
inspiration: 1690's reported pickup/orientation separation and installed dead spot motivate this proposal, not a geometry replica or performance claim.

states: UNTESTED heuristics; no physical pass. Pickup: nose down, rollers feed supported ramp. Hold: exit roll retains one coral in fixed V. Offer: release only to a ready receiver. Whole-robot occupancy blocks a second coral. Dashed ghost is a proposed nose stow position, not verified motion or a full sweep. Common bumper ring stays intact; an internal bellypan recess is optional, never a bumper cutout. Flat router-cut aluminum/polycarbonate, turned shafts and printed guide inserts; no accurate bends. All coordinates are approximate mm. Over y=-85..0, center z>=232 uses 165+57.15+9.85 mm; this is only a center-path heuristic, not full-length or 3D clearance. Traction, yaw, retention, loads and legality remain unknown.

title: Opposed belts and cradle
family: Short opposing belt runs lift into a fixed cradle
summary: An upper and lower belt run carry coral up a short incline, then offer it crosswise into a fixed supported cradle. UNTESTED proposal.
advantage: Opposed moving surfaces may maintain contact through the climb while a fixed cradle decouples pickup from receiver timing.
risk: Belt tracking, unequal speed and the floating upper mount can skew or pinch coral; the belt-to-cradle transition is unproven.
firstTest: Mock up both opposed belt runs with adjustable upper float; feed low-speed skewed coral and inspect exit support and jam reversal.
inspiration: 2056's reported jam-handling lesson and 6328's receiver-waiting lesson motivate this belt alternative; neither establishes this geometry or performance.

title: Floating nose and indexer
family: Four-bar pickup compliance with a stationary powered indexer
summary: A floating four-bar nose follows entry height while a supported bridge feeds a stationary indexer and low jaw. UNTESTED proposal.
advantage: The nose may accommodate floor variation without moving the indexer or changing the intended receiver pose.
risk: Four-bar motion changes the bridge gap and contact force; nose float can lift away from coral or hit the bumper.
firstTest: Move a flat-stock four-bar through small floor-height changes while hand-feeding coral; inspect bridge gaps, dead spots and hold pose.
inspiration: 6328's reported floating pickup and 1778's alignment-sensitive transfer motivate separating nose compliance from the fixed handoff; not a team replica.

title: Segmented star tunnel
family: Rotating star pockets advance coral beneath a compliant ceiling
summary: Three segmented star shafts step coral over slotted support guides under a floating ceiling, then offer it crosswise. UNTESTED proposal.
advantage: Discrete pockets may provide controlled low-speed advance while ceiling float accommodates changing contact geometry.
risk: Star phasing can pinch coral or leave an unsupported pocket transition; segment gaps may catch an end or deform the piece.
firstTest: Hand-crank three printed star stations under an adjustable ceiling; inspect offset coral, phase errors, pocket transitions and jam release.
inspiration: Original star-pocket alternative informed by 1690's dead-spot lesson and 2056's jam-handling reports; no claim that either team used this mechanism.
